William Kentridge

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We meet international acclaimed artist, William Kentridge, famous for his creative work in drawings, films, theatre and opera productions.

Unique Selling Point:
William Kentridge is an artist of black and white, a printmaker first, who uses drawing, animation, film, theatre, sculpture, opera, and even tapestry, to make compelling works that interrogate some of the darkest corners of history and the human psyche.
His practice is born out of a cross-fertilisation between mediums and genres and responsd to the legacies of colonialism and apartheid. His aesthetics are drawn from the medium of film’s own history from stop-frame animation to early special effects. Kentridge’s drawings, specifically the dynamism of an erased and redrawn mark, is an integral part of his expanded animation and filmmaking practice.


Summary:
William Kentridge was born on April 28, 1955 in Johannesburg to the parents of prominent apartheid lawyers. Kentridge remembers the sense of indignation and rage at the dinner table that was very formative.“My father was a prominent lawyer with prominent cases. He represented the family of Steve Biko and inquest into his death to the Sharpeville massacre. He was a lawyer in the treason trial of Nelson Mandela and other ANC members”.

Kentridge was captured in his own make-believe world as a child where drawing and play-acting was a metaphorical way of dealing with the political landscape and survive. “I did what all children do, and that is drew. And I simply forgot to stop, `` he remembers.

Kentridge studied Political Science and African Studies before studying art at the Johannesburg Art Foundation until 1978. There he met South African artists like Dumile Feni, whose works greatly influenced his drawings. Already working as a set designer for film productions, in 1981 Kentridge moved to Paris where he trained under the renowned mime artist, Jacque Lecoq. He then began making his signature hand-drawn animated films, made by filming a drawing, making erasures and changes, then filming it again.

He displayed his feelings about the two cities wryly in the title of his first animated film, "Johannesburg - Second Greatest City After Paris." "This is where I've lived for 55 years," he said, explaining how the city inspires him. "It is a city that deconstructs itself the whole time, it's busy erasing itself the way you erase a drawing." He admits to wondering why he has decided to make the city home. "There's certain sections of the city you drive down and think, why on earth do I choose to spend my days in this part of the world," he said. "And there are other days when you see extraordinary things and you think, this is remarkable."


Further information:
Kentridge's style is distinctive: His stark, bold charcoal drawings are characterized by frenetic bold black strokes. He also transforms many of his drawings into short animated films, using an idiosyncratic technique known as "stop-action animation." He will draw, erase and rework the same piece many times. Before he erases each version, he photographs it. Each photograph becomes a scene in the animated short film. He says his art is a constant work in progress and he rarely knows what the finished product will be. "You gradually arrive at the image, rather than know in advance and simply put it down," Kentridge said.

Kentridge's art, which has chronicled South Africa's shift from an apartheid to a post-apartheid society, evokes the tensions and memories of the former regime and reflects the inequalities of modern life. His work is inspired by a love-hate relationship with the gritty realism of his home city Johannesburg.

This artist, filmmaker and performer based in Joburg with a studio in Maboneng is one of the world’s most well-renowned artists with works at major art institutions and galleries globally. One of his most monumental recent works includes the 550-metre monumental frieze stencilled onto the wall overlooking the river Tiber in Rome (2016). In this open-air gallery Kentridge used a series of images taken from historical rome in addition to newer images of migrants arriving in italy today.

One of his recent works, The Head and the Load, (2018) is described by the Tate Modern as ‘Kentridge’s most ambitious work to date’. Combining music, dance, film projections, mechanised sculptures and shadow play, the exhibition tells the story of the millions of African porters and carriers who served the British, French and German forces during the First World War.

The head and the load comes from a proverb from Ghana meaning the head and the load are the troubles of one’s neck. So the load that one carries is your history, your personality. The subject of the piece is Africa in the First World War. the heads are mostly leaders of different colonial resistances. It has both an absurd and ridiculous element to it but also a part that will get right into the guts. It's about the specifics of the war, about colonialism, it's about incomprehension and making meaning.

In August the two of South Africa’s leading art institutions in Cape Town opened their doors to the largest William Kentridge exhibition in Africa. Why Should I Hesitate: Putting Drawings to Work, is staged at Zeitz Mocaa museum offering a wide survey of Kentridge’s work, including early word, as well as newer pieces on view for the first time in South Africa. It covers over 40 years of artistic production in drawing, stop-frame animation, video, prints, sculpture, tapestry and large-scale installation. The title references to Keentrdige’s primary practice of drawing, and how this core activity informs and enables his studio practice. It also references the impact of individual action on history and the reverse - how history shapes the contemporary and the future - and works as a commentary on various shifting hegemonies of power politics, economies, language and the authority to narrate history.

Running simultaneously at the Norval Foundation his three-dimensional sculpture work is on display spanning the past 19 years. Why Should I Hesitate: Sculpture will be first exhibition internationally to address Kentridge’s output as a sculptor. Covering several bodies of work, and testifying to his long standing and spontaneous improvisation when handling three-dimensional form, the sculpture exhibition at Norval sees the origins of these works in props: from his operas and images from his animations stepping off the stage and out of the screen, confronting us directly us ground level.

Our story
Set against the backdrop of Kentridge’s two current exhibitions at Zeitz Mocaa museum and the Norval Foundation in Cape Town the story will weave in and out of the exhibition space to the studio where the artist is at work.

Ideas are born in a studio. Kentridge takes us on his journey in a space he is most comfortable with: where ideas become art. His modest approach to his work is both refreshing and unusual to hear from an artist who has become a leading figure in the art world that will leave a legacy behind of an originator of ideas.

Collaboration is key in his projects. We hear from Catherine Meyburgh, the video and projection designer who has been working with Kentridge for the last 25 years more about the process and what it takes to bring together the different mediums into one show.

Art journalist, Sean O’Toole, who compiled the dense timeline of Kentridge’s work in the Mocaa catalogue has been following the artist career. His interview will give a different perspective of the artist's career he has been following.

We hear from the Senior curator at Zeitz Mocaa, Storm Janse van Rensburg, more about the exhibition where Kentridge’s work is showcased and how the project was put together.

All high resolution visual material will be available for the insert where we want to cross over from the art on display to the source material.

Kentridge’s Centre for the Less Good Idea is a non-commercial collaborative space hosted at Kentridge’s art studio in Maboneng that supports experimental and cross-disciplinary arts projects by bringing together artists, musicians, poets, dancers, actors and filmmakers to create new performative works. Nhlanhla Mahlangu , a singer, performer, dancer who has worked with Kentridge says “the centre is a safe space where we can dream without fear of failure”.

Final Script: Behind the scenes with William Kentridge
Duration: 8 minutes 10 seconds
Date: 25 October 2019

V/O William Kentridge – the man who never stopped drawing. Today, his artworks sell for millions, some is unobtainable. His stark black-and-white charcoal drawings have become signature pieces and have been turned into three dimensional works and put on stage.

Raised in the Sixties in Johannesburg to the parents of prominent anti-apartheid lawyers, the city built on gold became a metaphor for the political landscape and the absurdity of the world he lived in.

William Kentridge: South African Artist: It gave me a long term sense of the nature of social injustice and it gave me even more a sense of the unnaturalness of the Johannesburg I grew up in.

Masa Kekana: Would you say that this acute awareness is what prompted you to start drawing?

William Kentridge: I think all children draw. But by the age of 8 or 9 most children have outgrown that, I suppose I just forgot how to stop drawing.

V/O Kentridge’s career as an artist did not take off immediately. He studied African politics and dabbled in film and acting which he refers to as failures.

William Kentridge: So at the time they are suffered as failures even in retrospect you say how lucky I did all those different things that did not work that I feel at ease with actors and I feel at ease with film making. And now it is all part of the vocabulary that is used in the studio all the time.

Up sound

V/O Kentridge’s bold charcoal drawings became his signature pieces. They were transformed into animated films taking as much as 9 months to do a short film. Catherine Meyburgh edited most of his early animation films.

Up sound

Catherine Meyburgh: Video and Projection Designer: So he would quite often be working on a sequence or a couple of sequences, he will animate them and he will bring them to
me and then we will put them together and talk about it. It’s really very much an incredibly collaborative process but the films are really based on William’s animation and his thoughts of how he interacts with the world.

V/O In the early animated films, there is the stark reality of the political landscape; they’re an exploration of the darkest corners of our history.

Up sound

V/O From animated films, Kentridge moved on to larger works. Theatre and opera were natural progressions because he felt at home with performers and the creative team backstage. Meyburgh was brought in as projection designer to create the layered effect.

Up sound

Catherine Meyburgh: So the projections are to combine not only the live shadows with projections of either images we have already filmed and edited together and many layers of that with drawings and animations, live images that are projected so there is a combination of things.

Up sound

V/O One of Kentridge’s most ambitious projects premiered recently at the Tate Modern in London. The Head and the Load tells the story of the millions of African porters and carriers who served the British, French and German forces during the First World War. Kentridge combines music, dance, film projections, mechanised sculptures and shadow play in this large theatrical piece.

Up sound

V/O Other key collaborators include the composer Philip Miller, who has created the soundtracks for many of the artist’s pieces over the last 25 years, and more recently, the performer and musician, Nhlanhla Mahlangu.

Up sound

Nhlanhla Mahlangu: Composer and Theatre Maker: I joined the Head and The Load in season one of the Centre for The Less Good Idea and I joined as a dancer and in the process William discovered I am an actor as well and during the process he discovered I am a singer as well so I am an allrounder in the production.

Up sound

V/O The centre for the Less Good Idea is a collaborative space hosted by Kentridge’s art studio in Maboneng, Johannesburg that supports experimental and cross-disciplinary art projects.

Nhlanhla Mahlangu: The Centre for a Less Good Idea is a space where the artists are given an opportunity to dream and to create without the fear of failure.

V/O For Kentridge, the studio has always been the place where the world is invited into his dreams, thoughts and conversations. Now, for the first time on the African continent, two major galleries in Cape Town are showcasing Kentridge’s work in a retrospective spanning 40 years.

William Kentridge: There were 2 seperate invitations, one from the Norval foundation which is the first exhibition of sculpture so that for me was very interesting to suddenly see my work as sculpture and the Zeitz MOCAA as everything else which is installations, videos, drawings, prints. So obviously it is quite a radical compression of the work.

V/O Planning and preparation for the opening of the exhibition took months and required teams of designers and set builders to create the ideal exhibition space. Even Kentridge’s signature cat became a feature.

Up sound

Storm Janse van Rensburg: Senior Curator - Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art in Africa: Making an exhibition like this is a great challenge. How do you look at 40 years of work by a prolific artist and try and make sense of it that a visitor can come and experience it.

LINK: The exhibition here at Zeitz MOCAA of William Kentridge fills five independent spaces, starting here at the atrium, moving three floors, each highlighting a different aspect of his career.

Storm Janse van Rensburg: So it really starts from early drawings and early work and takes you on a journey to more recent pieces. So it is really inviting the visitor going on a journey through his life and his career.

V/O In a first-of-its-kind show, we see Kentridge’s sculptural work exhibited at the Norval Foundation. Many of the pieces originated as props form operas or as images from his animation series.

LINK: The gallery has reinforced floors to support the works, some weighing as much as 9 tons and reaching as high as 9 metres. From the technical design and construction of these new sculptures, Kentridge has collaborated with fellow artists in making this phenomenal new body of work.

Sean O’Toole: Art Critic - What he has the capacity to migrate a drawing into something bigger, be it a film, or with a set of sculptors or like in the Head and the Load. Very few artists have the capacity to take that ambition and to really scale it up.

V/O O’Toole has interviewed the artist many times and has recently written a chronological timeline of 40 years of Kentridge’s work for the Zeitz MOCAA catalogue.

Sean O’Toole: So I think someone coming to look at William’s exhibition, if they singularly think of him as an artist I think they are going to be missing out something. I always think of him as an artist director and it is in that wrestle that happens internally inside himself, which of those are more dominant, that his works express himself. And that is where his innovation as an artist lies.

V/O From the creator of his stark black-and-white charcoal drawings to becoming one of the most innovative sculptors in South Africa and internationally, Kentridge is constantly moving forward with new ideas.

William Kentridge: Sculpture for me is a larger question of what is in three dimensions and what is in two dimensions, like the cat over there. If it is in one position it is a cat but if you turn it around it turns into chaos and it resolves itself into a coffee pot so you understand it is not actually a cat but a massive mettle which from one angle is a cat and from everywhere else is chaos which is a methaphor of how we make sense of the world.

The man who never stopped drawing: his raw charcoal prints animated and given life on stage, William Kentridge has put South Africa on the global map of 21st century artists.

Today, his artworks sell for millions, some is unobtainable. His stark black-and-white charcoal drawings have become signature pieces and have been turned into three dimensional works and put on stage. Raised in the Sixties in Johannesburg to the parents of prominent anti-apartheid lawyers, the city built on gold became a metaphor for the political landscape and the absurdity of the world he lived in. William Kentridge: South African Artist: It gave me a long term sense of the nature of social injustice and it gave me even more a sense of the unnaturalness of the Johannesburg I grew up in. Masa Kekana: Would you say that this acute awareness is what prompted you to start drawing? William Kentridge: I think all children draw. But by the age of 8 or 9 most children have outgrown that, I suppose I just forgot how to stop drawing. V/O Kentridge’s career as an artist did not take off immediately. He studied African politics and dabbled in film and acting which he refers to as failures. William Kentridge: So at the time they are suffered as failures even in retrospect you say how lucky I did all those different things that did not work that I feel at ease with actors and I feel at ease with film making. And now it is all part of the vocabulary that is used in the studio all the time. Up sound V/O Kentridge’s bold charcoal drawings became his signature pieces. They were transformed into animated films taking as much as 9 months to do a short film. Catherine Meyburgh edited most of his early animation films. Up sound Catherine Meyburgh: Video and Projection Designer: So he would quite often be working on a sequence or a couple of sequences, he will animate them and he will bring them to me and then we will put them together and talk about it. It’s really very much an incredibly collaborative process but the films are really based on William’s animation and his thoughts of how he interacts with the world. V/O In the early animated films, there is the stark reality of the political landscape; they’re an exploration of the darkest corners of our history. Up sound V/O From animated films, Kentridge moved on to larger works. Theatre and opera were natural progressions because he felt at home with performers and the creative team backstage. Meyburgh was brought in as projection designer to create the layered effect. Up sound Catherine Meyburgh: So the projections are to combine not only the live shadows with projections of either images we have already filmed and edited together and many layers of that with drawings and animations, live images that are projected so there is a combination of things. Up sound V/O One of Kentridge’s most ambitious projects premiered recently at the Tate Modern in London. The Head and the Load tells the story of the millions of African porters and carriers who served the British, French and German forces during the First World War. Kentridge combines music, dance, film projections, mechanised sculptures and shadow play in this large theatrical piece. Up sound V/O Other key collaborators include the composer Philip Miller, who has created the soundtracks for many of the artist’s pieces over the last 25 years, and more recently, the performer and musician, Nhlanhla Mahlangu. Up sound Nhlanhla Mahlangu: Composer and Theatre Maker: I joined the Head and The Load in season one of the Centre for The Less Good Idea and I joined as a dancer and in the process William discovered I am an actor as well and during the process he discovered I am a singer as well so I am an allrounder in the production. Up sound V/O The centre for the Less Good Idea is a collaborative space hosted by Kentridge’s art studio in Maboneng, Johannesburg that supports experimental and cross-disciplinary art projects. Nhlanhla Mahlangu: The Centre for a Less Good Idea is a space where the artists are given an opportunity to dream and to create without the fear of failure. V/O For Kentridge, the studio has always been the place where the world is invited into his dreams, thoughts and conversations. Now, for the first time on the African continent, two major galleries in Cape Town are showcasing Kentridge’s work in a retrospective spanning 40 years. William Kentridge: There were 2 seperate invitations, one from the Norval foundation which is the first exhibition of sculpture so that for me was very interesting to suddenly see my work as sculpture and the Zeitz MOCAA as everything else which is installations, videos, drawings, prints. So obviously it is quite a radical compression of the work. V/O Planning and preparation for the opening of the exhibition took months and required teams of designers and set builders to create the ideal exhibition space. Even Kentridge’s signature cat became a feature. Up sound Storm Janse van Rensburg: Senior Curator - Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art in Africa: Making an exhibition like this is a great challenge. How do you look at 40 years of work by a prolific artist and try and make sense of it that a visitor can come and experience it. LINK: The exhibition here at Zeitz MOCAA of William Kentridge fills five independent spaces, starting here at the atrium, moving three floors, each highlighting a different aspect of his career. Storm Janse van Rensburg: So it really starts from early drawings and early work and takes you on a journey to more recent pieces. So it is really inviting the visitor going on a journey through his life and his career. V/O In a first-of-its-kind show, we see Kentridge’s sculptural work exhibited at the Norval Foundation. Many of the pieces originated as props form operas or as images from his animation series. LINK: The gallery has reinforced floors to support the works, some weighing as much as 9 tons and reaching as high as 9 metres. From the technical design and construction of these new sculptures, Kentridge has collaborated with fellow artists in making this phenomenal new body of work. Sean O’Toole: Art Critic - What he has the capacity to migrate a drawing into something bigger, be it a film, or with a set of sculptors or like in the Head and the Load. Very few artists have the capacity to take that ambition and to really scale it up. V/O O’Toole has interviewed the artist many times and has recently written a chronological timeline of 40 years of Kentridge’s work for the Zeitz MOCAA catalogue. Sean O’Toole: So I think someone coming to look at William’s exhibition, if they singularly think of him as an artist I think they are going to be missing out something. I always think of him as an artist director and it is in that wrestle that happens internally inside himself, which of those are more dominant, that his works express himself. And that is where his innovation as an artist lies. V/O From the creator of his stark black-and-white charcoal drawings to becoming one of the most innovative sculptors in South Africa and internationally, Kentridge is constantly moving forward with new ideas. William Kentridge: Sculpture for me is a larger question of what is in three dimensions and what is in two dimensions, like the cat over there. If it is in one position it is a cat but if you turn it around it turns into chaos and it resolves itself into a coffee pot so you understand it is not actually a cat but a massive mettle which from one angle is a cat and from everywhere else is chaos which is a methaphor of how we make sense of the world. ______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promos: 11 seconds In a rare interview, we are invited into the world of William Kentridge, who grants it was his failures that gave him the tools to turn stark black-and-white drawings into gripping theatre and opera. 11 seconds The man who never stopped drawing: his raw charcoal prints animated and given life on stage, William Kentridge has put South Africa on the global map of 21st century artists. 11 seconds In a rare interview with creative giant, William Kentridge, we meet the man who admits his failures gave him the tools to turn charcoal drawings into spectacular 21st century works of art. ____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We meet international acclaimed artist, William Kentridge, famous for his creative work in drawings, films, theatre and opera productions.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: William Kentridge is an artist of black and white, a printmaker first, who uses drawing, animation, film, theatre, sculpture, opera, and even tapestry, to make compelling works that interrogate some of the darkest corners of history and the human psyche. His practice is born out of a cross-fertilisation between mediums and genres and responsd to the legacies of colonialism and apartheid. His aesthetics are drawn from the medium of film’s own history from stop-frame animation to early special effects. Kentridge’s drawings, specifically the dynamism of an erased and redrawn mark, is an integral part of his expanded animation and filmmaking practice.
metadata.Summary: William Kentridge was born on April 28, 1955 in Johannesburg to the parents of prominent apartheid lawyers. Kentridge remembers the sense of indignation and rage at the dinner table that was very formative.“My father was a prominent lawyer with prominent cases. He represented the family of Steve Biko and inquest into his death to the Sharpeville massacre. He was a lawyer in the treason trial of Nelson Mandela and other ANC members”. Kentridge was captured in his own make-believe world as a child where drawing and play-acting was a metaphorical way of dealing with the political landscape and survive. “I did what all children do, and that is drew. And I simply forgot to stop, `` he remembers. Kentridge studied Political Science and African Studies before studying art at the Johannesburg Art Foundation until 1978. There he met South African artists like Dumile Feni, whose works greatly influenced his drawings. Already working as a set designer for film productions, in 1981 Kentridge moved to Paris where he trained under the renowned mime artist, Jacque Lecoq. He then began making his signature hand-drawn animated films, made by filming a drawing, making erasures and changes, then filming it again. He displayed his feelings about the two cities wryly in the title of his first animated film, "Johannesburg - Second Greatest City After Paris." "This is where I've lived for 55 years," he said, explaining how the city inspires him. "It is a city that deconstructs itself the whole time, it's busy erasing itself the way you erase a drawing." He admits to wondering why he has decided to make the city home. "There's certain sections of the city you drive down and think, why on earth do I choose to spend my days in this part of the world," he said. "And there are other days when you see extraordinary things and you think, this is remarkable."
metadata.Further information: Kentridge's style is distinctive: His stark, bold charcoal drawings are characterized by frenetic bold black strokes. He also transforms many of his drawings into short animated films, using an idiosyncratic technique known as "stop-action animation." He will draw, erase and rework the same piece many times. Before he erases each version, he photographs it. Each photograph becomes a scene in the animated short film. He says his art is a constant work in progress and he rarely knows what the finished product will be. "You gradually arrive at the image, rather than know in advance and simply put it down," Kentridge said. Kentridge's art, which has chronicled South Africa's shift from an apartheid to a post-apartheid society, evokes the tensions and memories of the former regime and reflects the inequalities of modern life. His work is inspired by a love-hate relationship with the gritty realism of his home city Johannesburg. This artist, filmmaker and performer based in Joburg with a studio in Maboneng is one of the world’s most well-renowned artists with works at major art institutions and galleries globally. One of his most monumental recent works includes the 550-metre monumental frieze stencilled onto the wall overlooking the river Tiber in Rome (2016). In this open-air gallery Kentridge used a series of images taken from historical rome in addition to newer images of migrants arriving in italy today. One of his recent works, The Head and the Load, (2018) is described by the Tate Modern as ‘Kentridge’s most ambitious work to date’. Combining music, dance, film projections, mechanised sculptures and shadow play, the exhibition tells the story of the millions of African porters and carriers who served the British, French and German forces during the First World War. The head and the load comes from a proverb from Ghana meaning the head and the load are the troubles of one’s neck. So the load that one carries is your history, your personality. The subject of the piece is Africa in the First World War. the heads are mostly leaders of different colonial resistances. It has both an absurd and ridiculous element to it but also a part that will get right into the guts. It's about the specifics of the war, about colonialism, it's about incomprehension and making meaning. In August the two of South Africa’s leading art institutions in Cape Town opened their doors to the largest William Kentridge exhibition in Africa. Why Should I Hesitate: Putting Drawings to Work, is staged at Zeitz Mocaa museum offering a wide survey of Kentridge’s work, including early word, as well as newer pieces on view for the first time in South Africa. It covers over 40 years of artistic production in drawing, stop-frame animation, video, prints, sculpture, tapestry and large-scale installation. The title references to Keentrdige’s primary practice of drawing, and how this core activity informs and enables his studio practice. It also references the impact of individual action on history and the reverse - how history shapes the contemporary and the future - and works as a commentary on various shifting hegemonies of power politics, economies, language and the authority to narrate history. Running simultaneously at the Norval Foundation his three-dimensional sculpture work is on display spanning the past 19 years. Why Should I Hesitate: Sculpture will be first exhibition internationally to address Kentridge’s output as a sculptor. Covering several bodies of work, and testifying to his long standing and spontaneous improvisation when handling three-dimensional form, the sculpture exhibition at Norval sees the origins of these works in props: from his operas and images from his animations stepping off the stage and out of the screen, confronting us directly us ground level. Our story Set against the backdrop of Kentridge’s two current exhibitions at Zeitz Mocaa museum and the Norval Foundation in Cape Town the story will weave in and out of the exhibition space to the studio where the artist is at work. Ideas are born in a studio. Kentridge takes us on his journey in a space he is most comfortable with: where ideas become art. His modest approach to his work is both refreshing and unusual to hear from an artist who has become a leading figure in the art world that will leave a legacy behind of an originator of ideas. Collaboration is key in his projects. We hear from Catherine Meyburgh, the video and projection designer who has been working with Kentridge for the last 25 years more about the process and what it takes to bring together the different mediums into one show. Art journalist, Sean O’Toole, who compiled the dense timeline of Kentridge’s work in the Mocaa catalogue has been following the artist career. His interview will give a different perspective of the artist's career he has been following. We hear from the Senior curator at Zeitz Mocaa, Storm Janse van Rensburg, more about the exhibition where Kentridge’s work is showcased and how the project was put together. All high resolution visual material will be available for the insert where we want to cross over from the art on display to the source material. Kentridge’s Centre for the Less Good Idea is a non-commercial collaborative space hosted at Kentridge’s art studio in Maboneng that supports experimental and cross-disciplinary arts projects by bringing together artists, musicians, poets, dancers, actors and filmmakers to create new performative works. Nhlanhla Mahlangu , a singer, performer, dancer who has worked with Kentridge says “the centre is a safe space where we can dream without fear of failure”.
